extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers and students) writing papers, notes, and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for writing clear, unambiguous mathematical prose, proofs, and LaTeX documents aimed at researchers and students preparing mathematics papers and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain source when a claim doesn't follow immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim does not follow immediately from the previous sentence alone, explain what it does follow from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Combining the previous two sentences shows that..."; "By Lemma 8.3, ..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Make justification clear for multiple claims in a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sentence contains more than one claim, make clear which reason is the justification for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, in a chain of equalities, make clear which reason explains which equality. Sometimes this can be effected by placing a reason before or after the chain of equalities, or by using \begin{align*} ... \end{align*} with a reason at the right in each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader should know why claims up to period are true
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader reaching the period of a sentence should know why each claim up to that point is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim's proof will come only after the period, indicate this by ending the sentence with something like ", as we now explain", or put the claim into a formal construction like \begin{lemma} ... \begin{proof} ... \end{proof}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate ambiguity in wording
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to write so that your words can be given the meaning you intend; write so that they cannot reasonably be given any other meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity should be eliminated even if it would cause only a minute of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long arguments into lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Break up long arguments by making parts of them into lemmas, even if the lemmas are used only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to minimize what a reader must keep in mind at one time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention which results are needed later
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section contains several theorems, propositions, and lemmas, but only one of them is needed in subsequent sections, mention this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can free up memory in the reader’s brain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantifiers unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Make quantifiers unambiguous: instead of writing ambiguous forms, write explicitly whether quantification is over all or some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: "We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for x ∈ R." or "We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S, x ∈ R." Good: "We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for all x ∈ R." or "We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for some x ∈ R."

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate where hypotheses are used in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should usually indicate where the hypotheses are being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise theorem/page numbers when citing
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a book or article, include a theorem number or page number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This should be omitted only when you really mean to cite the entire work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include version/date when citing arXiv preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing an arXiv preprint, include the version number or precise date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This way, even if a new version is uploaded, the reader can figure out what you were referring to. When citing a preprint elsewhere on the web, give the URL and date of the manuscript or date downloaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite forthcoming work only with public preprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite 'forthcoming work' only if there is a publicly available preprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: sometimes the work doesn't appear or is delayed, and announcing it can discourage others from working on the problem; see AMS Policy Statement on Ethical Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theorem statements short; definitions first
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep theorem statements short. Definitions should precede the theorem in which they are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentences short and combine only for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep sentences short. Combine sentences (with ", and" or with a semicolon) only if it helps to clarify the logic or if the sentences are otherwise closely related.

rubrics_metrics.name: String equalities/inequalities into a single chain
rubrics_metrics.description: If an argument involves combining several equalities, string them together in one chain of equalities (in the correct order!), if possible; same for inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can make the logic easier to follow since everyone understands transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction should reach main results early
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction to an article should get to new and interesting theorems as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is OK to postpone definitions to a later "Notation" section (and to refer readers in the introduction to this later section) if those definitions are standard enough that most readers will be able to read the introduction without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do easier parts of proofs first when breaking into parts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof breaks into parts, do the easier parts first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify explicit maps when claiming isomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that two objects are isomorphic, specify the map between them explicitly (at least in one direction) and claim that that map is an isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start induction at the convenient base case
rubrics_metrics.description: Start induction arguments with base case n = 0 instead of n = 1 if it is easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing 'clear' without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually when people write that something is 'clear', it is because they could not figure out a good explanation of why it is true. If it really is clear, it is usually not necessary to say that it is clear. If it is not clear (or even if it is), then try to say a few words to give the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define variables before they are needed; avoid ', where...' construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of the ", where..." construction, in which explanations of notation come after the notation is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, define variables before they are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the subject of a sentence part inside a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a sentence or clause cannot consist of words outside a formula together with a fraction of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: "For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant ∆ = b^2 − 4ac." Better: "For a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant ∆ equals b^2 − 4ac."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abbreviations like WLOG, iﬀ, s.t.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use abbreviations like WLOG, iﬀ, and s.t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those are for blackboard use only, if at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical symbols outside formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use logical symbols such as ∃ and ∀, unless you are writing about formal logic and they appear in a logical formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, write out ∃ as "there exists" (or "there exist"), and so on. See [CMOS, 12.5].

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a sentence with a symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a bad full sentence: "H denotes the Sylow p-subgroup of G." (should not appear as a full sentence)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contractions in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions such as "don't" in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs over contradiction when equally easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a proof by contradiction when a direct proof would be just as easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to theorems by number, not by position words
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to theorems by number instead of writing "the previous theorem", "the proposition above", and the like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use single numbering system for theorems/lemmas/etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single numbering system for all theorems, lemmas, etc., instead of having both a Theorem 1.1 and a Lemma 1.1 in the same paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes statements easier to find and can help prevent citation errors. LaTeX solution: put \newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[section] then \newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}, etc. (Presumes amsart or similar; otherwise \usepackage{amsthm}.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare operators in LaTeX for correct spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: To get correct spacing for operators like Gal, declare them in the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use \DeclareMathOperator{\Gal}{Gal} once in the preamble and \Gal in the body each time you need it. (Presumes amsart or similar; otherwise \usepackage{amsmath}.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent misalignment of enumerate items with \hfill
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \hfill before \begin{enumerate} if necessary to prevent misalignment of the first item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: avoid misaligned items in Theorem statements like (a),(b),(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \colon for map notation spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of f : X \to Y, use f \colon X \to Y for appropriate spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare spacing between the two forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try \usepackage{fullpage} to save manual margin settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{fullpage} in the preamble to fit more on a page without having to set margins manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try microtype package to reduce bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{microtype} just before your \begin{document} to allow LaTeX to adjust spacing between characters to reduce the number of bad line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider colonequals package for := notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have mastered everything else, try \usepackage{colonequals} in the preamble and \colonequals as needed in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare := and := carefully!!!

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'so that' vs 'such that' correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: The words "so that" convey purpose, whereas "such that" just imposes a condition. Each instance of "so that" should be replaceable by at least one of "in order that" and "with the result that".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good: "We include 0 in N so that N contains the size of every finite set." Bad: "An abelian group is a group so that every two elements commute."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'A, so B' for implication
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are trying only to indicate a logical implication between statements A and B, write "A, so B" instead of "A, so that B" or "A, and so B".

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'only' close to the word it modifies
rubrics_metrics.description: The word "only" should be placed as close as possible to the word it is modifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See [Kil07] for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'Given an element g of G' over 'Given g an element of G'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of "Given g an element of G" write "Given an element g of G".

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Theorem' when referring by number
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to a theorem (or proposition or section or ...) by number, capitalize the word "Theorem".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "By Section 3.4 and Theorem 5.6, the proposition holds."; "By Faltings’s theorem, X(Q) is finite."

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain punctuation around displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying a formula does not change the punctuation required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Instead of "By Theorem 3.2, we have:

Gal(L/K) ≅ Z/2Z × Z/2Z" write "By Theorem 3.2, we have

Gal(L/K) ≅ Z/2Z × Z/2Z."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Assume that' for full clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: "Assume G is a finite group." should be "Assume that G is a finite group."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the other hand, "Assume Hypothesis A." is OK. Similarly, "Assume n ≥ 1." is OK because "n ≥ 1" serves as a noun unit. Same rules for "Suppose". See [Wes15] for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid '1980's' style; use '1980s'
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to the 1980s, not the 1980’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See [CMOS, 9.34].

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow punctuation rules for i.e. and e.g.
rubrics_metrics.description: I.e. and e.g. should be followed by a comma, at least in American English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also, if what come before and after are full sentences, then the i.e. or e.g. should be preceded by a semicolon instead of a comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize parentheses; omit when traditional
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of parentheses. For instance, log x is better than log(x), and it is traditional to omit parentheses also in some expressions like sin 2x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But in sin(x + y), parentheses are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usually omit centered dot for multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually it is not necessary to use a centered dot or other symbol for multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write (n + 1)(n + 2), not (n + 1) · (n + 2) or (n + 1) × (n + 2). If both factors are numbers, however, juxtaposition would be confusing, so write 3 · 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit filler phrases like 'We remark that' when unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Filler words like "We remark that" and "Note that" should be omitted, except when their absence would produce a sentence starting with a symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't restate end-of-proof if QED symbol used
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof ends with an end-of-proof symbol, then it is not necessary to write "This concludes the proof." or "Thus we are done."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slash for fractions in exponents/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fractions in exponents or subscripts should use the slash instead of being stacked vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write x^{3/2}, not x^{3\over2} or similar stacked forms. (Reference [CMOS, 12.47].)

rubrics_metrics.name: Write sequences as ordered tuples, not sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as an ordered tuple is written (2, 3, 5) instead of {2, 3, 5}, a sequence should be written (a_i)_{i≥0} instead of {a_i}_{i≥0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefix 'non' usually does not need a hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefix "non" does not need a hyphen when it appears in common words such as nonempty, nonnegative, nonsingular, nontrivial, and nonzero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference [CMOS, 7.85].

rubrics_metrics.name: Most numbers in math papers should be numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Most numbers in math papers should be written as numerals instead of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: If it is a single-digit number being used only as a counting number instead of a mathematical quantity, then it may be spelled out as a word. Example: "These two genus 2 curves are isomorphic." Note: Some authors write small numbers as words in more situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'since' over 'as' for causal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically it is OK to use "as" as a synonym for "since", but this usage sounds stilted and can make sentences harder to parse because of other possible meanings of "as".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, "since" should be preferred. Example of egregious usage: "As x does not tend to +∞, the expression e^x is bounded."

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'per' when you mean 'by'
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly, do not use "per" when what you mean is "by".
